paragraphs.text: P. van den Berg
Psalm 133: 1–3; Ephesians 4: 1–3; John 17: 17–23

I desire, dear brethren, to speak of spiritual dignity in the last days. As we have said already, the testimony is marked by the dignity of the anointing. We could not think of a more dignified position than to be in an environment that is equal to having the divine presence.

What dignity is involved in that!—the divine system, the anointed system, and the service in it marked by the anointing. The blessed Holy Spirit has formed an order of things that is equal for the divine presence, and it is filled; the divine presence is in the assembly, the habitation of God in the Spirit, and the service of God is in it, the priestly service as marked by the anointing.

So there is a great realm of things where God is being served according to His own thoughts in the light of what He Himself has set out for His own pleasure, and we are thankful to be in the days we are in, thankful for the way God in His grace has granted a revival at the end of the dispensation in order that He might have for Himself a practical answer to His original thoughts; for God never reverts to second thoughts. He stands by His original thoughts, even at the present time in the day of small things. There is one Spirit, and there is one body, which is still here, and the great thing for us is to be marked by the dignity of what we have been called into, because the calling of God today is what it was at the beginning; there is a sanctified position here, and it is maintained by the Minister of the sanctuary.

So we have a presentation in Psalm 133 of this glorious Person, typified in Aaron, and in a sense the whole dispensation is seen. What was seen in the high priest of old was a representation of the dispensation; there was a change when the high priest died, and you get a kind of picture of the dispensation in the Priesthood of Aaron. Of course, the Person we are speaking of is a Priest according to the order of Melchisedec; which shows the exceeding greatness of the Person of Christ, He has neither beginning of days nor end of life (Hebrews 7: 3). He is eternal in His own Person. Then, following the order, there is the function of the priesthood, and I think in Aaron we have the function, marked by the dignity of the anointing.

Christ is the Man of God’s pleasure, the anointed One. It says “Grace is poured into thy lips”, Psalm 45: 2. Think of the way it was expressed; when He opened His mouth words of grace went forth. A brother was saying to me that it used to be said that grace is love in activity away from home. I am just passing it on because it is very affecting. Think of it, dear brethren, we being here and the activity of grace, love active away from home. So we have ‘The Person of the Christ, enfolding every grace’. We have the picture here of Aaron and the remarkable connection with brethren dwelling together in unity.

What a wonderful thing it is that God has given us a revival at the end that is marked by brotherly affection; affections for one another. The Holy Spirit having come, and the love of God being shed abroad in our hearts by Him, the practical answer in the power of the Holy Spirit is in brotherly affections marked by life, indeed it involves eternal life.

Eternal life is not an individual matter, it is collective enjoyment, it is what we enjoy in the company of one another in an altogether different world, an out-of-the-world condition. It is a world where Christ the Priest has gone in and our interests are bound up with that glorious Person in the place where He is. It works out in a practical sense here as we are in the gain of our place with Christ in glory, the One who is Firstborn among many brethren, the One to whom we are united, our glorious Head. As we enjoy relations with Him where He is, and are in the good of that together, there will be in evidence what we have here, brethren dwelling together in unity. That is, as John says, “We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brethren”, 1 John 3: 14. It is a practical matter—we love the brethren; John makes a great point of that in his ministry. John is God’s reserve for the last days, and shows how divine affections are found here company-wise in God’s own family, those who are together in family relations. They are not brought together on social lines; they are not persons who have chosen one another in any sense, but those who have been set together in the grace of God in the light of the truth and with whom it is our privilege to work out what is for the divine pleasure in the testimonial setting, and in the service of God.

So it says, “How good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!”. It can only be on the basis of departing from iniquity—separation from evil is God’s principle of unity. We could not enjoy unity together if there was evil present; we could not enjoy unity if the truth was not our bond. What brings us together is the truth; the test in the last days is the truth, and the truth puts us in the testimony and is our bond. The testimony is marked by this descending character of things. The Holy Spirit descended upon Jesus, and He came down when the church was formed. What marks christianity is what is coming down out of heaven, a wonderful order of things here that has its origin in heaven, but it is coming down out of heaven. Finally the city in administration in the world to come is seen coming down out of heaven. Whilst it is here, it is really in a heavenly position marked by coming down out of heaven, and that is just what is here in the assembly, it is an order of things that is marked by what is of heaven. “For both he that sanctifies and those sanctified are all of one” (Hebrews 2: 11); their origin is all of one.

There is a holy company here, a sanctified company, sanctified by the truth, sanctified by the Spirit’s presence, and marked by the features that were seen in Jesus, the heavenly Man, the Man out of heaven, who moved here as One who was from heaven. That is how Jesus was here; what marked Him was lowliness, the descending line, and that is where God is working at the present time, dear brethren, in our minds—the mind which was in Christ Jesus. If you want to know where God is moving, it is not in proud minds, it is not in obstinate minds, it is in subject minds, lowly minds. The sound of marching in the tops of the mulberry-trees (2 Samuel 5: 24) indicates the way God is moving in the mind that was seen in Christ Jesus, and thus there is victory. There is the line of the testimony that will go through in victory in this lowly attitude of mind, the mind that was in Christ Jesus, the One who in that mind maintained the rights of God and completed the testimony which the Father had given to Him. What a privilege it is, dear brethren, to be found available to the Lord at the close of the dispensation, and to find things running on in spiritual dignity, the oil descending upon Aaron’s beard, the dignity that would be presented in it, and then going on to the hem of his garments, showing how things will go through to the close.

The hem of Aaron’s garments is the finish, it shows how things in this character, on a descending line, will go through to the end, to the completion of the dispensation. What marks the hem of Aaron’s garments is the pomegranates and the bells; that is to say, there is what is seen in the light of the assembly in local companies, the pomegranates. I think that would be connected with what the Lord says at the end, ‘ I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify these things to you in the assemblies’, (Revelation 22: 16), in the plural. So that at the end of the dispensation there are the twos and the threes, perhaps in the smallest outward conditions, but seen as set together as pomegranates, an ordered setting of things. I think the Lord has concern for local assemblies, to see that there is conformity, to see that there is no independence, no congregationalism, amongst us; we would not think in one locality differently from what our brethren are thinking elsewhere; we are to be governed by divine principles.

The Lord has His own rights in the local assembly, which are not to be interfered with, each standing on its own ground in its own responsibility to Him, and yet marked by what is seen in the gates of the heavenly city. Each gate of one pearl means that every local assembly represents what the mind of God is in relation to the assembly and that what is held in the place is what is due to God in the light of the whole; we are governed by the same divine principles, the truth as we have received it. It has been the subject of combat in the course of the testimony, but it has come through, dear brethren, and we want to keep the charge that has been given to us in maintaining in every local assembly what answers to the assembly, maintaining what is due to God in relation to it. We have the priesthood of Christ to support us, to see us through; the living line of the testimony will go through, and then the bells would show that there is a testimony. Nearly every departure from the truth amongst the saints in the last one hundred and fifty years has been followed by people going in for gospel activity so-called, because assembly ground was lost. But the great thing that God has, and His prime interest at the present time, is the assembly, and you can only have the gospel rightly when you have the assembly rightly. So it is very important to hold that ground, and to be in the good of what the Lord is saying currently to the assemblies; then you find that something of bridal character, so pleasing to Christ, comes to light, the Spirit and the bride, the bride being in perfect keeping with the speaking of the Holy Spirit, and saying the same thing, ‘Come’.

So it says, “Let him that hears say, Come”; I think that is the bells. There is a testimony to our fellow believers, whom we have in our hearts, dear brethren, whom we love. We have them in our hearts and affections and we long to see them come into what we are enjoying, a revival in our day, that God has granted His people food, that He has given them a blessing.

We want others to come into it so that “him that hears” would no doubt refer to other believers. Let them say, Come; let them say what we are saying through grace, and “he that will” would be the way that the glad tidings would go out; you have something that you can bring people into; you have a realm of salvation where persons are safe, where God has His own thoughts, the assembly being the pillar and base of the truth. God wants all men to be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Timothy 2: 4). You want to see that there is something that you can bring them into, what is here in the light of the assembly, and is available even in days such as this because, as we have already said, God does not revert to second thoughts because of the departure; He stands by His original thoughts.

I thought that in Ephesians we would be greatly stimulated to see the light of this. We are exhorted by the Lord’s prisoner, who was in outward circumstances of great limitation and weakness, as indicated in Paul’s chain (2 Timothy 1: 16). I trust that we are not ashamed of Paul’s chain. Onesiphorus went all through Rome to find Paul and he was not ashamed of Paul’s chain. We would long for other believers that they might find Paul today, what Paul represents, the Lord’s elect vessel. I am referring to the distinct Pauline line of truth that has come through to us so distinctively in the revival and the way that it is available today. We long to see our fellow believers being prepared to take on the position of reproach that is connected with the man in prison, Paul’s chain. Paul says the word of God is not bound (2 Timothy 2: 9); the choicest thoughts of God came out from that prison. The whole counsel of God, as it came out at Ephesus in his ministry, entered into what Paul wrote in the epistle to the Ephesians, and he is exhorting us to walk worthy of the calling wherewith we have been called.

The point is spiritual dignity, to walk worthy, according to Psalm 133, in the dignity of the anointing, in the dignity of the heavenly calling, recognising the spiritual formation in each one functioning as joints of supply in order that there may be the development of what is for God in one another in the bringing in of what is spiritual, and getting through to what is spiritual in one another, so that we get the increase of the body to its self-building up in love (Ephesians 4: 16). So Paul says, “with all lowliness and meekness, with long-suffering”

This is the mind that was in Christ Jesus, involving that our hearts and minds have been affected by the descending path of Jesus. We are learning from Him who is meek and lowly in heart and are finding rest for our souls. There is no rest if we are fighting amongst ourselves, devouring one another, but there is rest for our souls in this going down mind, and we will find that it will make way for this unity, “the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace”. The unity of the Spirit can never be broken; the uniting bond of peace can be broken.

So we have to see to our relations one with another, that the golden clasps and the loops of blue are getting hold of one another, as it says, “that the tabernacle may be one”, Exodus 27: 6. That is the concern of the apostle here; he says, “There is one body and one Spirit”, not, there was one body and one Spirit, but there is one Spirit and one body.

Now as to John 17, we have often been reminded that John is God’s reserve in the last days and we have, we might say, the High Priest presented to us in the holiest. The Lord Jesus in speaking to the Father in verse 11 says, “Holy Father, keep them in thy name which thou hast given me, that they may be one as we”. Think of the oneness between the Father and the Son—“I and the Father are one”, John 10: 30. The Holy Spirit is involved, dear brethren. He is the bond between the Father and the Son, and He is the bond between Christ Jesus and His own, as Mr. Raven taught us. I am not just speaking about unity here, I am speaking of oneness because there is more than unity between divine Persons; there is oneness. Unity is connected with our side, but when we speak of divine Persons they are infinitely one; ‘all are God, all one God, God all three’, as Mr. Darby said (N.S. Vol. 32, p.16).

So we have the Lord’s words here, “Sanctify them by the truth—thy word is truth”, and the Lord is serving in view of presenting the assembly to Himself without spot or wrinkle, or any of such things. Sanctification by the truth involves that we are set apart from all that is in the world and brought into holy relations one with another. If there is worldliness how can we expect to be in this oneness?—but the assembly is an order of things that has nothing to do with the world, she is an unworldly witness here of heavenly things; her origin is heaven, her destiny is heaven; she is just passing through here, and the thing for us is to be marked by this oneness, “that the world may believe that thou hast sent me”. We must own our part in the public breakdown in christendom, but there is something that the Lord has, and which John contemplates, of Bethany character. There is a testimony; the Jews said, “Behold how he loved him!”, John 11: 36. The world saw a testimony at Bethany. Well, the Lord has something of Bethany character in the present time, and He desires that it might exist in our relations with divine Persons, with the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, that we might be marked by this oneness, and by these affections, taking character from the way that Christ was in the affections of the Father and the Father in the affections of Christ, all involving the blessed Holy Spirit.

These things are to be true in His own, that we by the Spirit might be in the flow of divine affections. I desire to be more in it myself, to know more of this current flow of divine affections operating and taking in the assembly, a vessel that is so near the Trinity, the vessel that is so near to God in revelation, and which is soon to come out of heaven having the glory of God. Dear brethren, what oneness there is in the heavenly city, the climax of God’s own work in the present time coming

out, not marked by breakdown but by what is altogether glorious, and by oneness, it has one street. So we would desire, dear brethren, that we might be characterised by the dignity that belongs to it. The departure from the truth that has taken place resulted in dignity being set aside and things being brought down to the level of the world, but what God has for Himself is marked by spiritual dignity. May we be preserved in the light of our heavenly calling, and walk worthy of the calling wherewith we have been called, in the oneness seen in the relations between the Father and the Son, the Spirit of His Son being sent out into our hearts whereby we cry, Abba, Father. So the Lord says, “The glory which thou hast given me I have given them, that they may be one, as we are one”, that is the glory of sonship. Oh that we might be one, even as Christ is one with the Father; the many brethren are the many sons being brought to glory, and the many brethren are all of one. May the Lord help us in the light of these thoughts, dear brethren, to be here for His own pleasure and to be effectual here in His testimony, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: A CHEERFUL GIVER AND CHEERFUL GATHERINGS
articles.author: E. C. Muggleton

paragraphs.text: What is in mind in reading these scriptures is to speak about giving, a cheerful giver, and cheerful gatherings. You will notice the word that “God loves a cheerful giver”. Now I think every one of

us in the assembly should be a cheerful giver. God Himself is the great Giver. We need to think of God as the Giver of all good, and He is the great Blesser, too. It says, “He who, yea, has not spared his own Son but delivered him up for us all, how shall he not also with him grant us all things?”, Romans 8: 32. What a wonderful impression, beloved brethren, to have of God, that He spared not His own Son. So when we think of giving, we think of God as the great Giver who “so loved the world”, as it says in John 3: 16, “that he gave his only-begotten Son, that whosoever believes on him may not perish, but have life eternal”. So we love to think of God having a world in which He is going to find His pleasure eternally, not a world of confusion or strife, but a world that is entirely suited to Him, a world that is centred in His beloved Son. As the Son of God He is the centre of God’s world and God is drawing our hearts in affection to Christ so as to have this before us.

I think the Lord has helped us as to the thought of giving and how the assembly is to take on this feature. What lies behind it is what is sacrificial. I believe all giving has its true basis in what is sacrificial. That is why I referred to Romans 8, “He who, yea, has not spared his own Son, but delivered him up for us all”. Think of the sacrificial basis upon which God will secure, through Christ, a universe that will be responsive to Him eternally. So we read, “God, having sent his own Son, in likeness of flesh of sin, and for sin, has condemned sin in the flesh”, Romans 8: 3. Christ came in in that way and God condemned sin in the flesh in regard of the work of Christ, and it was in order that the righteous requirement of the law should be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to flesh but according to Spirit. God loves to take account of His people according to Spirit.

I think the Lord would help us to see what is established in the statutes that Moses brought to Israel. We have in the beginning of Deuteronomy the statutes and ordinances that Moses spoke to all Israel. God has only one standard of things before Him and the statutes that have been laid down for us by the Lord in the ministry of those who have led in the recovery are for the whole assembly. The word “take heed” comes into Deuteronomy 12 six times. One word is “Take heed to thyself that thou offer not thy burnt-offerings in every place that thou seest; but in the place which Jehovah will choose in one of thy tribes, there thou shalt offer thy burnt-offerings, and there thou shalt do all that I command thee”, Deuteronomy 12: 13, 14. Now we are to think of the commandments; we are reminded of what Paul says, “If any one thinks himself to be a prophet or spiritual, let him recognise the things that I write to you, that it is the Lord’s commandment”, 1 Corinthians 14: 37. So the statutes are for all Israel and then we have, too, in Deuteronomy 12: 19, “Take heed to thyself that thou forsake not the Levite all the days thou shalt be in thy land”. Now, beloved brethren, that was laid down in the ministry of our beloved brother Mr. Taylor, that we should not forsake the levite. How wonderful it is that God can bring us round to these statutes so that no tribe is to be out of accord with them. How pleasing it is to God to see the saints moving in their tribes, moving in unity in relation to a statute that has been laid down.

What I have in mind in referring to this scripture is what God loves, and one thing He loves is a cheerful giver. Of course there are other things that God loves; He loves the gates of Zion more than all the habitations of Jacob (Psalm 87: 2). He loves our dwellings; He loves to be with us in our dwellings, but He loves the gates of Zion even

more. Who would fail to come up with his offering on the first day of the week? We should come with our offerings to the place “which Jehovah your God will choose to cause his name to dwell there”, Deuteronomy 12: 11. Now we are not to go to any place that we see, we are not to compromise, we are to move here as those who are true to the fellowship to which God has called us. It is the fellowship of His Son and it is to be the place which Jehovah shall choose to cause His name to dwell there. There is only one place; there is only one fellowship; there is only one loaf, one body. So God has in mind the unifying of the saints in relation to His statutes that are laid down for the whole assembly.

Then we are to “take heed to hear all these words which I command thee, that it may be well with thee, and with thy children after thee for ever, when thou doest what is good and right in the eyes of Jehovah thy God”, Deuteronomy 12: 28. We can say, beloved brethren, that it is good and right that we should minister to the levites. It is an obligation of love, and I think basically it lies in the spirit of sacrifice. God loves a cheerful giver and what is given is to be dedicated for a specific purpose. The Lord has helped the saints in their giving to minister to the levites, that the work of the ministry and the work of the glad tidings, which is one matter, should go on unhindered and that the servants should be free to move and to minister to the saints. Now that is very pleasing to God and behind it all lies this thought that God loves a cheerful giver. We can think of the giving of Christ and the giving of God. What giving! And we are to be imitators of God, according to Ephesians 5: 1; “Be ye therefore imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love”. I think that is the Deuteronomy setting, that we are to walk in love, we are to be formed in the divine nature, so that we move together in accord
with what is laid down for us in the ordinances and statutes for all Israel.

Now we know the two ordinances of christianity, one is baptism and the other the Lord’s supper. We are to pay attention to these things, for the Lord has commanded them, and we are to do “what is good and right in the eyes of Jehovah thy God”. If we are on this line we are pleasing to God. He loves to see the saints moving tribally in relation to these things. And then it says in the last verse of Deuteronomy 12, “Everything that I command you, ye shall take heed to do it; thou shalt not add thereto, nor take from it”. May we bear the word, ‘Take heed to do it’. It is not only that the Lord gives us light—and how we appreciate the help that came in in beloved Mr. Taylor’s time—but “Ye shall take heed to do it”.

Now I come to “cheerful gatherings”, and I think our gatherings, dear brethren, should be cheerful. I read from Zechariah because you will remember, in relation to the people coming out of captivity and the rebuilding of the temple, how they were stimulated and encouraged, and how they prospered, through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah. Now we are thankful for the ministry meeting, and the prophets who speak God’s mind. We are glad to hear His voice and we are to take heed to it. God has His prophets; He has had them since the world began.

Now we come to this prophet Zechariah. Jehovah’s word comes to His servant. It says in Zechariah 8: 1, “And the word of Jehovah of hosts came unto me, saying, Thus saith Jehovah of hosts—I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great fury.
Thus saith Jehovah—I am returned unto Zion, and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem; and Jerusalem shall be called, The city of truth; and

the mountain of Jehovah of hosts, The holy mountain”. So we have been reminded of the assembly of God in a place, that it is a holy assembly and it is a holy fellowship. Do not let us lower the standard. God in His mercy brought Israel and guided them, according to Exodus 15, to the abode of His holiness, the place that He chose to put His name there. And that is where we are to bring our offerings. Let us see that we are coming to that place, the place of the abode of His holiness. It is like the assembly in the wilderness.

When we come to Zechariah 8: 6 you get the word again, “Thus saith Jehovah of hosts—If it be wonderful in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be wonderful in mine eyes? saith Jehovah of hosts. Thus saith Jehovah of hosts—Behold, I will save my people from the east country and from the west country; and I will bring them, and they shall dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in truth and in righteousness”. How wonderful it is that we can be in truth and in righteousness in this day of so much departure from it. “But now I will not be unto the remnant of this people as in the former days, saith Jehovah of hosts; for the seed shall be prosperous, the vine shall give its fruit, and the ground shall give its produce, and the heavens shall give their dew; and I will cause the remnant of this people to possess all these things”

(Zechariah 8: 11, 12). We are thus in a wonderful time. God is causing the dew to come, and the ground yields its produce; God loves prosperity and the people prospered through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah. God will have a prosperous people—He loves the thought of prosperity. He is so rich in the way He blesses us, rich in mercy. We have the rich, unlimited character of God’s giving and of His blessing towards

us. He loves to bless His people and God is blessing them today, causing the ground and the seed to be prosperous—“the vine shall give its fruit, and the ground shall give its produce, and the heavens shall give their dew”. We are to be encouraged in these things. There is an area in the local assembly that is prosperous and this prosperity is in the hearts of the saints.

You will remember that in John’s third epistle his great desire as to Gaius was “that in all things thou shouldest prosper and be in health, even as thy soul prospers”. God loves the thought of soul prosperity, and what lies behind it is sacrifice; it is the fruit of the sacrifice of God, and the sacrifice of Christ—how we love to think of the burnt-offering, the character of His giving, and then of how Christ loved the assembly and delivered Himself up for it. God would have us to be here walking in love, even as Christ loved us and delivered Himself up for us, an offering of sweet-smelling savour to God (Ephesians 5: 1, 2). God has also a sweet-smelling savour in the sacrificial offering of the saints, and I believe it enters into what is dedicated in their material giving as well. May the Lord strengthen us in this.

Then I come to Zechariah 8: 18, “And the word of Jehovah of hosts came unto me, saying, Thus saith Jehovah of hosts—The fast of the fourth month and the fast of the fifth, and the fast of the seventh, and the fast of the tenth, shall be to the house of Judah joy and gladness, and cheerful gatherings”. May there be cheerful gatherings in our localities. I think the saints should not be held up by all the breakdown and confusion that we find around us; our gatherings should take on the features of joy and gladness. “Love ye then truth and peace”.
May the Lord strengthen us in this desire. I believe

He has been helping us in regard of these matters, that we should observe the statutes that are laid down for us in the Scriptures. God has great pleasure in seeing His people coming together and being joyful and having cheerful gatherings, unified together in what is for His own heart, all being based on the wonderful sacrifice of Christ through which all will be brought to pass for the pleasure of God eternally in the vast universe of bliss.

May we be obedient to what God has laid down for us, the ordinances and the statutes that are for all Israel, and thus be prospered together in unity, “For there hath Jehovah commanded the blessing, life for evermore”, Psalm 133: 3. Let us use diligence to keep the unity of the Spirit in the uniting bond of peace—truth and peace are to be in our gatherings.

Brethren dwelling together in unity is “like the precious oil upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, upon Aaron’s beard”. May we thus be encouraged, and the brethren helped, in doing what is pleasing to God, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: HOW AFFECTION FOR CHRIST IS DEVELOPED
articles.author: Dr. S. D. K. Roberts
scriptures: 2 Samuel 19: 30; Song of Songs 5: 16 (first clause); John 13: 23; Genesis 37: 3

paragraphs.text: I have been considering, in relation to the longings of my own heart—and I am sure that they are in the hearts of my brethren—how our love for Christ may be increased. It has been said in these meetings that it is love for Christ which would stimulate us to go in for heavenly and eternal things. We are attracted ‘over Jordan’ to where Christ is. How, then, can that love for Him be increased?
It seems to me that there are certain lines of contemplation that the Holy Spirit would use to this end. First, there is the contemplation of Christ’s grace toward each one of us.

Mephibosheth’s love for David was developed, I believe, along this line. Think of what David had done for him. He had extricated him and given him a place at his own table as one of the king’s sons. Has not the Lord Jesus done this for each one of us? The contemplation of His grace toward us endears Him to us “The charm of a man is his kindness”, Proverbs 19: 22. Let us, dear brethren, maintain a sense of Christ’s grace—let us not lose it. Why should He pick me up, or you, and bring us into blessing? Mephibosheth showed his love for David in his readiness to give up all to be where David was. He says, “Let him”—that is, Ziba—“even take all”. It is the power of appreciation of Christ that would cause us to relinquish things here and to move over to where He is.

Then I was thinking of the excellence of His Person suggested in the Song of Songs. The feminine speaker is engaged with the personal excellency of her lover; “Yea, he is altogether lovely”. She is not thinking of what he has done for her but of what he is to her. Think of the power of attraction there is in Christ. It is illustrated in the sun holding the planets. The whole moral universe will be held in the power of attraction to the face of Jesus. What a contemplation!
Then there is the contemplation of His love.

John in the passage read is speaking about himself as a disciple ‘in the bosom of Jesus, whom Jesus loved’. John knew Christ’s love for him and, as we know, love begets love. Every believer can take account of himself as a disciple whom Jesus loves. Love for Christ is developed as we contemplate Christ as loving each of us personally, not by thinking of our love for Him. Each one of the myriads surrounding Him in a coming day will have a personal consciousness of His love and as looking on Christ will be able to say, ‘He loved me and gave Himself for me’.

The last scripture portrays a father’s love for his son. I think love for Christ is developed in us as we contemplate the love that the Father has for the Son. As loving the Father we love the One whom He loves. We are called to share the love that the Father has for Him who is in His bosom.

So, dear brethren, I believe love for Christ is developed in us by the Holy Spirit along these lines—by the contemplation of His grace, of His personal excellence, of His love, and then of Himself as the Son of the Father’s love.

articles.title: REDEMPTION
articles.author: C. Middleton
articles.place: Because “we have redemption through his blood”.

paragraphs.text: The christian, counting blessings that are his,
May learn how wonderful redemption is,
‘Redemption in Christ Jesus’ now is known
Because for him the Saviour did atone.
The judgment which he would have had to face
Is all removed since Jesus took his place,
And bore that solemn judgment in his stead,
And on the cross His precious blood was shed.
That blood that saved him from the judgment sword,
Ensures he’s now belonging to the Lord,
Bought with a price, no longer now his own,
No rights have any but the Lord alone.
Freedom from Satan’s power, the world, and sin,
The evil that’s without and what’s within;
The One who died for him and made him whole
Has now the right to have him in control.
Now God is free in all His thoughts to bless,
Which He can do in perfect righteousness,
And all accusing voices must be still—
He can with those redeemed do what He will.
The malefactor by the Saviour’s side
Learned what redemption meant ere Jesus died,
No power of evil then could bar the way
To be with Him in paradise that day.
And we now left to tread the path below,
The present power of redemption know,
Not of the world, nor yet are we our own,
We are the Lord’s—what joy when this is known.
That daily we can prove His gracious care
Until He comes and takes us to Him there,
With Him within the Father’s house above,
That is our place, prepared by Him in love.
Blessed with all blessings in the heavens above,
God thus effecting what He planned in love;
We thus know sonship’s wondrous place with God

Peter in Matthew 16 and 17 represents material that is of special value to the Lord. Not only did He have the Father’s revelation concerning: the Person of Christ and answer for the company to the question, “But ye, who do ye say that I am?”, but he merits the Lord’s severest rebuke in the section following, directing him to the path of discipleship, and suffering in which the Lord Himself led. Later he was to lose his life for Christ and find it. He would have his reward in the coming kingdom.

Though rebuked in chapter 16, he is selected foremost by the Lord in chapter 17 to be a witness of His glory on the mount of transfiguration. The Lord’s investment in Peter was fully justified at Pentecost and in his service which followed. As ‘Peter’, he was of the same material as the rock upon which the assembly, unassailable because of its foundation, was built. So it will remain, for none can assail the great work of Calvary and the risen Son of God. If the Lord must needs suffer, yet He would rise the third day and the whole counsel of the enemy would be overthrown. The assembly as built by Christ, not man, can never be conquered. We too, can have this full confidence that the Lord’s work is going through.
Kingston, Ont.

GOD KNOWN IN JUDGMENT In Psalm 9 David says, strikingly, “Jehovah is known by the judgment he hath executed”. We need constantly to contemplate the sufferings of Christ. At the cross we see God’s judgment executed on all that was obnoxious to Him, and sustained by Christ. We learn God in His holiness, in the glory of His righteousness, and in His grace and mercy. We see God’s judgments in history also. In His dealings with Israel, with nations, and with kings (such as Nebuchadnezzar) we learn God as He deals with principles, such as disobedience, idolatry, and self-exaltation, which challenge His rights. In church history, too, God has come in at many points in judgment, making manifest what is evil, and sustaining what is right. We are to learn Him through these crises and to be obedient to His will as thus clearly made known.

Let us be like the writer of Psalm 119 who says, “Thy judgments have I set before me” (Psalm 119: 30); “Thy judgments are good” (verse 39); “I have not departed from thy judgments; for it is thou that hast taught me” (verse 102); “1 have sworn … that I will keep thy righteous judgments” (verse 106); “Every righteous judgment of thine is for ever” (verse 160); “Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments” (verse 164), and, finally, “Let thy judgments help me” (verse 175).

Now, beloved brethren, I would appeal to you. I believe that we have come to a crisis. There is a crisis in the souls of God’s people at the present time. We have arrived at a place where two roads meet; the one leads straight to heaven, and the other leads into the world. It leads gradually, admit, but it leads there, and it is for you to make up your mind which way you are going to tread. The Lord is bent on placing us in possession of the inheritance. The daughters of Zelophehad said, ‘We want an inheritance amongst our brethren’, and they got it. May God grant that that, too, may be the desire of every one of us. Not a fine business, nor a status in the world, but an inheritance amongst our brethren, where Christ is the centre and sun.

You do not fear death, because Christ has the keys of death and hell. He is the vessel of divine power. You do not fear the devil, because Christ has got the power over the devil. He will shut him in the abyss. So I do not fear the world because Christ has overcome the world
… Being raised from the dead He is the vessel of divine power. He exercises all divine power.
The poem on page 19 was received from our beloved brother, Mr. Charles Middleton, a few days before the Lord took him on 30 July 1977.
